implementation_notes: Scala has the keyword: `lazy val index = buildIndex()` initialises on first access and the compiler emits the synchronisation needed to publish the value safely to all threads (a bitmap-and-offset scheme; Scala 3 uses a different initialisation algorithm designed to avoid holding locks while running user code), so user code contains no marker, no lock and no double check. It replaces the whole classic structure, and the two eager alternatives are `val` (built with the enclosing object) and `def` (rebuilt every access). `lazy val` is write-once, so recomputable laziness is expressed with a memoised collection or a Future instead, and the compiler's cost is per lazy val (bitmap plus a synchronised prologue).
pitfalls: Initialisation order: a lazy val whose initialiser reads another lazy val of the same instance can deadlock across threads (two threads each holding one side of the pair), and reading a later-defined plain val sees its default value (null/0).
Marking a value @threadUnsafe (Scala 3) or publishing it through a plain var removes the guarantee: racing first accesses can run the initialiser twice or expose a partially built value.

Every lazy val costs a bit in the class's bitmap and a synchronised prologue on first access, so classes with dozens of lazy vals (or lazy vals in hot value classes) pay for the mechanism even when it is never contended.

Overriding a lazy val with a val (or vice versa) changes the initialisation contract silently, and abstract lazy vals are a Scala 3-only feature - inherited code that relies on them does not compile on Scala 2.

variants.name: lazy val with the @threadUnsafe escape hatch (Scala 3)
variants.implementation_notes: Scala 3 lets a lazy val opt out of the synchronised scheme: @threadUnsafe switches to a faster mechanism that is not thread-safe, which is the language's version of Kotlin's LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE. Use it only for values confined to one thread and where profiling shows the default scheme's prologue matters - usually in hot data classes with many lazy fields. It is a contract change, not an optimisation: the flag documents that the enclosing instance is never shared, and the tradeoff is a possible double initialisation or a partially built value under concurrency.
pitfalls: The annotation buys a cheaper prologue at the price of the publication guarantee: if the instance escapes to another thread (a cache, a shared Future callback, a static) the value can be built twice or observed half-built.
Nothing in the type system or the compiler flags a later change of concurrency model, so the annotation survives refactors that invalidate its premise.
Mixing @threadUnsafe and normal lazy vals in one class means different fields have different initialisation semantics, which is invisible at the use site.
